I’ll develop the single most novel part of the seed: the **bristle-embedded debris sensor** that detects debris/plaque by electrical resistance changes. I’m not developing the optional micro-needle tips, gamification, or eco-material angle except where they naturally support the core sensing/cleaning function.

---

## GlossGuard Pro — Bristle-Level Impedance Debris-Mapping Toothbrush

### 1. Selected concept and physical principle

The seed proposes that tiny sensors embedded in toothbrush bristles could detect debris by changes in **electrical resistance**. That is physically plausible, but raw DC resistance measurement in a wet, moving, foam-filled mouth would be noisy, unstable, and could cause electrode polarization or electrochemical effects.

So the invention preserves the seed’s core paradigm — **bristles themselves are local electrical sensors** — but implements it as **local AC impedance spectroscopy** using a coaxial micro-bristle electrode. The “resistance change” described in the seed becomes the **real part of the impedance at low frequency**, while the full impedance spectrum provides a robust way to distinguish debris/plaque from saliva, toothpaste foam, enamel, and metallic fillings.

The key physical idea:

- Tooth enamel is a high-impedance mineral surface.
- A thin acquired salivary pellicle is relatively insulating and capacitive.
- Dental plaque/biofilm is an ionic, water-rich gel containing bacterial cells, extracellular polymers, and dissolved salts; it has stronger ionic conduction and a characteristic dielectric response.
- Food debris is more irregular, often conductive and mechanically mobile, producing rapidly fluctuating impedance.
- A very small electrode gap — about 5–10 µm — samples only the surface-bound layer at the bristle tip, so the measurement is naturally localized to the tooth surface rather than the whole mouth.

---

### 2. Novel physical coupler: the coaxial impedance micro-bristle

A practical embodiment is a **coaxial sensing bristle**, or “CIMB”: a flexible bristle-like probe that has two electrodes at its tip.

#### Structure of one sensing bristle

| Layer | Material | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Core electrode | 25–50 µm diameter Pt/Ir alloy or Pt-coated 316L | Inner working electrode |
| Dielectric gap/spacer | 5 µm parylene C | Insulating gap between core and outer electrode |
| Outer ring electrode | Au/TiN-coated polyimide or PEEK tube, outer diameter ~150 µm | Counter electrode |
| Outer insulation | 10–15 µm parylene C or medical-grade TPU | Electrically insulates the bristle shaft; only the tip face is exposed |

At the tip, the coating is polished so that the face exposes a small central electrode and an outer ring electrode separated by the 5 µm insulating gap. Current flows from the core, through the overlying salivary/debris/plaque layer, into the outer ring.

Because the electrode gap is only ~5 µm, the electric field at the tip is confined to roughly that same distance. This is the crucial engineering trick: the sensor does not see the whole mouth, only the material immediately under the bristle tip. This makes it possible to build a local “debris map” during brushing.

The sensing bristle is slightly softer or slightly recessed, about **0.2 mm shorter** than the surrounding cleaning bristles, so it contacts the tooth when the bristle field is pressed against the surface but does not act as a scrubbing element.

---

### 3. Brush head architecture

The replaceable brush head contains:

- **12 coaxial sensing bristles** distributed in three rows: near the toe, mid-head, and heel.
- Each sensing bristle is surrounded by ordinary nylon cleaning bristles for mechanical support and cleaning.
- A thin polyimide flex circuit embedded in the brush head routes the core and outer-ring leads of each sensing bristle to spring contacts at the head–handle interface.
- 12-channel analog multiplexing is located in the brush head or neck to reduce wiring complexity.

The handle contains:

- An impedance/vector front end, e.g. an AD5941-class impedance spectrometer.
- A microcontroller with Bluetooth 5.0, e.g. nRF52840.
- A 6-axis inertial measurement unit for rough brush-position tracking.
- A rechargeable 3.7 V Li-ion battery and sealed brush motor.
- Optional haptic motor for real-time physical feedback.

---

### 4. Measurement protocol

The system measures local impedance at each sensor bristle during brushing.

#### Operating parameters

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Excitation amplitude | ≤100 mV rms |
| Current limit | ≤5 µA rms |
| Frequencies | 10 kHz, 50 kHz, 100 kHz, 250 kHz, 500 kHz |
| Per-channel sampling rate | ~20 Hz |
| Number of sensing channels | 12 |
| Full scan cycle | ~0.6 s |
| Wireless latency | <100 ms |

These electrical levels are far below any nerve or muscle stimulation threshold and are safe for intraoral use.

#### Contact detection

A reading is accepted only when the high-frequency impedance magnitude falls into a plausible contact range, for example:

- **Open air / no contact:** \(|Z|_{100\,\text{kHz}} > 1\,\text{M}\Omega\)
- **Intimate tooth contact:** \(|Z|_{100\,\text{kHz}} \approx 500\,\Omega\)–\(1\,\text{M}\Omega\)

This prevents the system from misinterpreting air gaps or foam bubbles as tooth contact.

---

### 5. From impedance to debris detection

For each accepted contact event, the system extracts:

- \(|Z|\) at 10 kHz and 100 kHz
- Phase angle \(\theta\) at 10 kHz and 100 kHz
- Real part \(R\) at low frequency — this is the seed’s “resistance change”
- Ratio \(|Z|_{10\,\text{kHz}} / |Z|_{100\,\text{kHz}}\)
- Short-time variability of the impedance signal

The classification logic is trained using ex vivo measurements on extracted teeth, artificial saliva, S. mutans biofilms, food debris, toothpaste, and common restorative materials.

Typical expected signatures:

- **Clean enamel with salivary pellicle:** higher impedance magnitude, more capacitive phase, stable signal.
- **Plaque/biofilm:** lower impedance magnitude, more resistive phase, and a characteristic frequency-dependent change due to ionic conduction and bacterial cell membranes.
- **Food debris:** low impedance, but rapidly fluctuating because particles move under the bristle.
- **Toothpaste foam:** typically resistive and low-phase; can be rejected as a background state using the multi-frequency phase behavior.

The output is a **debris/plaque likelihood score** per brushing zone, not a simple resistance number.

---

### 6. Debris heat map and user feedback

The handle’s IMU provides approximate brush orientation and position. Sensor readings are assigned to rough zones:

- Upper/lower
- Left/right
- Buccal/lingual
- Gumline/interproximal/occlusal

The app aggregates repeated contact events and builds a **Debris Heat Map**, as in the seed. If a zone remains high after several seconds, the handle vibrates or the app says: “Focus on the back molar gumline on the upper right.”

A useful balance: the system is not claiming millimeter-level dental mapping, but it can identify missed regions and guide the user much better than a timer can.

---

### 7. Key engineering challenge and how it is solved

The main challenge is that a wet mouth, saliva, toothpaste foam, and mechanical motion make simple electrical resistance measurement unreliable.

The solution is threefold:

1. **Coaxial micro-bristle geometry**  
   The 5 µm electrode gap confines the measurement to the surface layer at the tip, preventing the whole mouth from acting as a conductive shunt.

2. **AC impedance spectroscopy**  
   AC measurements avoid polarization and electrochemical damage. Multi-frequency data separate capacitive clean enamel from conductive plaque and resistive foam.

3. **Repeated-contact statistical mapping**  
   Because brushing is dynamic, no single reading is used alone. The system requires several high-quality contacts in the same zone before marking it as clean or debris-covered. This rejects motion artifacts, air bubbles, and brief accidental contacts.

---

### 8. Materials and safety

- **Tooth-contact materials:** Pt/Ir, parylene C, Au/TiN, medical-grade TPU — all compatible with ISO 10993 biocompatibility testing.
- **Cleaning bristles:** standard nylon 612 or PBT, rounded tips.
- **Electrical safety:** DC isolation capacitors between electrodes and battery; current-limited excitation; no direct current path into the mouth.
- **Mechanical safety:** sensing bristle tips are rounded and slightly recessed; no sharp micro-needles are used.
- **Waterproofing:** handle and head are IP67 sealed.
- **Replacement:** brush heads are replaceable every 3 months, like a normal toothbrush head.
- **Regulatory path:** as a hygiene/wellness product initially; plaque-detection claims would require clinical validation and potentially dental-device regulatory approval.

---

### 9. Prototyping pathway

A realistic prototyping sequence would be:

1. Fabricate individual coaxial sensing bristles using wire coating, parylene deposition, and tip polishing.
2. Mount them in a fixture and test against extracted teeth in a 37°C oral phantom.
3. Create known surface states: clean enamel, salivary pellicle, S. mutans biofilm, food debris, toothpaste slurry.
4. Train the classifier to separate these states.
5. Integrate sensors into a modified electric toothbrush head.
6. Run a small human feasibility study comparing the app’s Debris Heat Map against conventional plaque disclosing tablets and clinician Plaque Index.

---

### 10. Concrete utility advantage over existing approaches

Existing electric toothbrushes measure **time and pressure**, but they cannot detect where debris or plaque actually remains.

Disclosing tablets reveal plaque, but they are messy, post hoc, and not practical for daily use. Intraoral cameras require stopping and are expensive.

GlossGuard Pro’s real advantage is that it closes the loop **during brushing**: it senses the surface directly, through saliva and foam, and tells the user whether a zone is actually clean or still debris-laden. That is especially valuable for:

- Patients with braces, implants, crowns, or gum disease.
- Children learning adequate brushing.
- Elderly or disabled users with reduced dexterity.
- Anyone who wants an objective “is this area clean?” signal instead of guessing.

The core mechanism — a bristle-level coaxial impedance sensor — makes the seed’s “electrical resistance debris detection” physically practical, safe, and potentially manufacturable.

**Selected seed concept:** Adaptive Bristle Technology — piezoelectric nanofiber bristles that adjust stiffness/pressure based on debris type. I’m deliberately leaving aside the separate optical/electrochemical sensing, app, hydrogel strip, and eco-housing features; the sensing needed here is done by the same piezoelectric bristle layer.

---

# GlowClean Pro Adaptive Piezoelectric Bristle Array

## 1. Core idea

The brush head contains six independently controlled zones of active bristles. Each active bristle is a coaxial piezoelectric composite fiber. By changing the electrical impedance across the piezoelectric layer, the brush can electronically tune the effective bending stiffness of the bristles in each zone. The same piezoelectric layer, when briefly switched into sensing mode, detects the mechanical “signature” of the surface being brushed — soft biofilm, food film, early mineralized plaque, or relatively healthy enamel/gingiva — and selects the appropriate stiffness.

This preserves the seed’s unusual paradigm: the bristles themselves adapt their stiffness/pressure based on debris type.

## 2. Bristle architecture

Each active bristle is built as a coaxial fiber:

| Layer | Material | Thickness / diameter |
|---|---:|---:|
| Core | Medical-grade nylon 6,12 monofilament | 90 µm |
| Inner electrode | PEDOT:PSS or Ti/Au | ~200 nm |
| Piezoelectric layer | Aligned electrospun PVDF-TrFE nanofibers, poled in the radial direction | 18 µm |
| Outer electrode | PEDOT:PSS or conductive elastomer | ~300 nm |
| Insulation | Parylene C, FDA-compatible | 2 µm |

Total bristle diameter is around **125–130 µm**, with a length of **8–10 mm**. The piezoelectric layer is thicker and sits farther from the bending axis than the core, so it contributes substantially to the overall bending stiffness.

A brush-head zone is about **4 mm in diameter** and contains **30 active bristles**. All piezoelectric layers in a zone are connected in parallel to one control circuit. This gives practical spatial resolution without requiring individual bristle-level electronics.

## 3. Key engineering challenge: making “stiffness change” physically real

A simple piezoelectric polymer fiber cannot change its Young’s modulus by a large factor just by applying a DC voltage. The open-circuit versus short-circuit stiffness difference in PVDF-TrFE is only on the order of 1–2%, because the electromechanical coupling coefficient \(k_{31}\) is small.

The invention solves this with a **controlled-impedance shunt**, specifically a stable switched negative-capacitance circuit.

The effective axial compliance of the piezoelectric layer depends on the electrical admittance \(Y\) connected across its electrodes. Qualitatively,

\[
s_{\text{eff}} = s_{11}^{E} - \frac{d_{31}^2}{\epsilon_{33}^{T} + Y}
\]

where \(s_{\text{eff}}\) is the effective elastic compliance of the piezoelectric layer. By using a negative-capacitance circuit with

\[
C_{\text{neg}} \approx -0.7\, C_p
\]

where \(C_p\) is the piezoelectric capacitance, the denominator becomes small and the electrically induced compliance change is strongly amplified. The circuit is operated below the stability boundary, with a phase margin greater than 10°, to prevent self-oscillation.

Practical result:

- In **soft mode**, the effective modulus of the piezoelectric layer is driven toward a very low value, so the bristle bends easily.
- In **firm mode**, the piezoelectric layer is shunted with open circuit or a small positive capacitance, making it stiffer.

Because the piezoelectric layer contributes roughly 60–70% of the composite bristle’s bending stiffness, this gives a clinically meaningful overall stiffness change of about **2–3×** between soft and firm modes.

## 4. Sensing: how the bristles know the debris type

The same piezoelectric layer works in direct piezoelectric mode: when a bristle bends, it produces a small charge. The brush switches a zone into **sense mode** for short intervals, typically 50 ms per zone, and reads the bending waveform with a charge amplifier.

Signal bandwidth: **1 Hz–10 kHz**  
Sampling rate: **20 kS/s per zone**

Mechanical signatures:

- **Soft biofilm / food film:** low high-frequency energy, smooth viscoelastic recovery, low RMS amplitude.
- **Early mineralized plaque / hardened deposit:** sharp high-frequency transient spikes, higher 1–10 kHz energy, irregular contact events.
- **Healthy enamel/gingiva:** smooth low-amplitude baseline.

A lightweight on-device classifier extracts features such as spectral centroid, RMS, zero-crossing rate, high-frequency energy ratio, and cepstral coefficients. It updates the stiffness decision every **100 ms**, so the brush adapts while the user is brushing.

## 5. Operating modes

| Mode | Electrical state | Bristle behavior | Use case |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Sense | High-impedance charge amplifier | Passive bending sensing | Detecting debris type |
| Soft | Negative capacitance \(C_{\text{neg}}\approx -0.7 C_p\) | More compliant, gentle | Gums, exposed dentin, soft plaque |
| Firm | Open circuit or small positive capacitance | Stiffer, more scrubbing action | Early mineralized plaque, occlusal surfaces |
| Failsafe | Short circuit / electronics off | Standard soft-nylon behavior | Safety |

Because bristle stiffness changes, the same hand force produces lower interfacial pressure in soft mode and higher local pressure in firm mode. The brush does not need to apply dangerously high force; it changes the mechanical response of the bristles.

## 6. Safety and practical limits

- Maximum applied voltage: **±10 V**.
- Current limit: **<100 µA per zone**.
- The piezoelectric layer is fully encapsulated in parylene C; no electrode contacts oral tissue.
- A leakage-current monitor shuts off the active electronics if leakage exceeds **5 µA**.
- All materials are lead-free and medical/food-contact grade: nylon, PVDF-TrFE, PEDOT:PSS, parylene C.
- Firm mode is equivalent to a **medium** toothbrush, not an aggressive hard brush.

Important clinical caveat: the device does **not** claim to remove established dental calculus/tartar. That requires professional scaling. It detects and targets the harder, early mineralized deposits and plaque before they progress, and avoids over-pressuring soft tissues.

## 7. Utility advantage over existing approaches

Standard toothbrushes force a trade-off: soft bristles are gentle but less effective on hard plaque; medium/firm bristles clean better but increase risk of gingival recession, abrasion, and over-brushing.

Existing smart toothbrushes mostly track brushing time, motion, and sometimes pressure. They do not change the mechanical properties of the bristles themselves.

This invention changes bristle stiffness locally and automatically:

- **Gentle on gums, tongue, exposed dentin, and implant margins.**
- **Firmer on occlusal surfaces and early mineralized plaque.**
- **Real-time adaptation** based on mechanical tissue/debris feedback.
- **Same piezoelectric layer** acts as sensor and variable-stiffness material, avoiding separate fragile optical or electrochemical sensors.

The target users are people with gingivitis, orthodontic appliances, implants, exposed dentin, and anyone who brushes too hard or misses hard-to-clean zones.

## 8. Prototyping path

1. **Single-fiber validation:** Fabricate coaxial piezoelectric-coated nylon fibers and measure bending stiffness versus shunt impedance, including negative capacitance.
2. **Zone-level head:** Build a six-zone brush head with 30 active bristles per zone and a flexible interconnect to the handle.
3. **Signal collection:** Collect piezoelectric bending signatures from dental models and human volunteers to train the debris classifier.
4. **Electronics integration:** Miniaturize the impedance-control circuits, charge amplifier, and safety monitor into a rechargeable handle.
5. **Clinical testing:** Compare plaque removal and soft-tissue safety against standard soft and medium manual brushes.

# Bristle-Level Opto-Impedance Plaque-Detecting Toothbrush  
**Core concept developed from the seed:** the “micro-debris sensing brushes” — not the UV-C, fluoride coating, or gamified app features.

---

## 1. What is being developed

The seed’s most unusual and valuable idea is that the **bristles themselves** detect debris, plaque, and biofilm in real time, and the brush responds locally. This is a major departure from standard electric toothbrushes, which at best have a timer, a global pressure sensor, and maybe an app that tracks arm movement. Those devices do not know whether plaque is actually present.

The physically realizable version of the seed is a brush head containing **dedicated sensor bristles**:

- **Optical-fiber bristles** detect plaque by autofluorescence.
- **Conductive polymer bristles** detect plaque/debris by local impedance changes.
- A local piezo actuator in each zone of the brush head responds when debris is detected.

This preserves the seed’s paradigm: the sensor is **in the bristle**, not a camera looking at the mouth.

---

## 2. Why the original seed needs a physical coupler

The seed says “each toothbrush bristle is embedded with tiny optical sensors and capacitive sensors.” Literally instrumenting all ~1,000 conventional nylon bristles is not manufacturable: individual bristles are typically 0.15–0.20 mm wide, and each one would need an optical path, electrical contacts, and signal routing.

The engineering solution is to use a **sparse array of real sensor bristles**:

- A small number of bristles are themselves **polymer optical fibers**.
- A small number are **conductive elastomer/nylon bristles**.
- The remaining bristles are ordinary nylon cleaning bristles.

This gives bristle-level sensing where it is useful, without requiring impossible wiring of every bristle.

---

## 3. Physical sensing principles

### 3.1 Optical detection of plaque by autofluorescence

Dental plaque contains bacterial porphyrins — such as protoporphyrin IX and coproporphyrin — produced by bacteria including *Porphyromonas*, *Prevotella*, and *Actinomyces*. These porphyrins absorb blue-violet light around **405 nm** and re-emit red fluorescence in the **600–700 nm** range.

Healthy enamel has very weak red fluorescence. Therefore, if you illuminate a tooth with 405 nm light and measure the red/blue ratio, you get a useful surrogate for plaque and biofilm presence.

This is not a new lab principle — it is the basis of quantitative light-induced fluorescence, or QLF, used in dental research and clinical caries/plaque detection. The invention moves QLF from a bulky dental-office camera into a toothbrush bristle.

### 3.2 Capacitive/impedance detection of debris and biofilm

Plaque and food debris are hydrated, ion-containing materials. They behave electrically as an **ionic hydrogel** rather than a dry dielectric.

Clean enamel has relatively low permittivity and low ionic conductivity. A biofilm or debris layer increases local capacitance and lowers impedance at low-to-mid frequencies.

By placing two conductive bristles close together and driving a small AC current between them, the local impedance changes when the bristles contact plaque or debris instead of clean enamel. This provides a second, complementary sensing channel that can also detect non-fluorescent food residue.

---

## 4. Concrete architecture

### 4.1 Brush head layout

The brush head is divided into **six sensing zones**, corresponding roughly to:

1. Buccal/lower left  
2. Buccal/lower right  
3. Buccal/upper left  
4. Buccal/upper right  
5. Occlusal/lingual posterior zone  
6. Anterior/lingual zone  

Each zone contains:

- **One central optical sensor bristle:** a single multimode polymer optical fiber, core diameter about 250 µm, outer diameter about 275–300 µm, numerical aperture ≈ 0.5.  
- **Two or three conductive bristles:** carbon-loaded nylon monofilaments, diameter about 0.18 mm, coated with parylene C except for the last 0.5–1.0 mm at the tip.  
- **Ordinary nylon cleaning bristles** surrounding the sensor bristles.

The optical fiber tip is **recessed approximately 0.3 mm** behind the cleaning-bristle tips. This means it does not directly scrape enamel, but it is close enough to optically interrogate the tooth surface through a thin film of saliva or water.

The conductive bristles are flush with the cleaning bristles so they make gentle electrical contact with the tooth or debris.

### 4.2 Sensor bristle materials

**Optical fiber bristle:**

- Core: PMMA or a low-loss polymer optical material with good blue transmission.  
- Cladding: fluorinated polymer.  
- Jacket: thin polyurethane or polyimide for mechanical protection.  
- Tip: polished flat and sealed with a transparent biocompatible polyurethane or epoxy cap.

PMMA polymer optical fiber has acceptable attenuation at 405 nm over the short length used here — roughly 1–3 cm. Since the optical path is only a few centimeters, even moderate blue attenuation is negligible.

**Conductive bristle:**

- Base material: carbon-loaded nylon, which is flexible and conductive.  
- Insulation: parylene C, a biocompatible, water-resistant polymer.  
- Exposed conductive tip: 0.5–1.0 mm.

### 4.3 Optical engine in the handle

The handle contains:

- **405 nm LED**, not a laser.  
- A short-pass dichroic beamsplitter that reflects 405 nm excitation into the optical fiber and transmits longer-wavelength fluorescence.  
- A **silicon photodiode** with a 600 nm long-pass filter for red plaque fluorescence.  
- A second photodiode with a 405 nm bandpass filter to measure reflected excitation light for normalization.  
- A 1×6 optical switch or micro-mirror array that sequentially addresses each of the six sensor fibers.

The LED is modulated at **10 kHz**. Lock-in detection rejects ambient room light and motion noise.

### 4.4 Impedance front end

Each conductive bristle pair is connected to an impedance-spectroscopy ASIC, such as an AD5933-class device, through pogo pins or a molded interconnect.

Operating parameters:

- Frequency: **50 kHz and 1 MHz**  
- Voltage: **100 mV RMS**  
- Current limit: **<10 µA**  
- Measurement: complex impedance magnitude and phase  

The current is strongly limited so that the user is never exposed to anything more than a very small local sensing current.

### 4.5 Local actuation

Each of the six zones has a small piezoelectric disc at its base:

- Material: PZT-5A  
- Diameter: **5 mm**  
- Thickness: **0.2 mm**  
- Drive: **200–400 Hz**  
- Displacement: **15–25 µm**

When a zone’s sensor detects plaque above threshold, the handle increases the piezo vibration in that zone. The main brush motor continues normal global brushing, but the targeted zone delivers additional mechanical stimulation.

### 4.6 Data processing

For each zone, the handle computes:

\[
Plaque\ Index = \frac{I_{red}}{I_{405} + I_{green}}
\]

Where:

- \(I_{red}\) is fluorescence collected through a 600 nm long-pass filter.  
- \(I_{405}\) is reflected excitation light.  
- \(I_{green}\) is optional autofluorescence from clean enamel, used to improve specificity.

A zone is classified as “needs attention” when the plaque index exceeds a calibrated threshold, typically **1.3–1.5 times the clean-enamel baseline**.

The impedance sensor provides a second score:

\[
Debris\ Index = \frac{C_{50kHz} - C_{baseline}}{C_{baseline}}
\]

When both optical and impedance signals suggest plaque/debris, the system triggers local piezo vibration and marks the zone on the app.

---

## 5. How the bristle-level optical fiber works in practice

The optical fiber is not just a light pipe. It is the sensing aperture.

During brushing:

1. The 405 nm LED sends modulated light through the fiber.  
2. The light exits the polished fiber tip and strikes the tooth surface a short distance away.  
3. If plaque is present, bacterial porphyrins absorb 405 nm and emit red fluorescence.  
4. Some of that red fluorescence is collected back through the same fiber.  
5. The dichroic beamsplitter sends the red component to a photodiode.  
6. The signal is normalized against reflected 405 nm light to account for tip-tooth distance and saliva.

This is a **fiber-optic fluorescence probe**, but packaged as a bristle.

The conductive bristles work as a local impedance probe. When the bristle tips touch plaque or debris, the measured capacitance and resistance change because the hydrated biofilm has different electrical properties than clean enamel.

---

## 6. Key engineering challenges and solutions

### Challenge 1: You cannot put a sensor in every nylon bristle

**Solution:** Use a sparse array of dedicated sensor bristles. The optical fiber itself is the “optical sensor bristle,” and the conductive carbon-loaded nylon is the “capacitive sensor bristle.” Ordinary cleaning bristles remain passive.

### Challenge 2: The mouth is wet, foamy, and optically noisy

Toothpaste foam, saliva, and motion can scatter light and reduce signal quality.

**Solutions:**

- Modulated 405 nm LED with lock-in detection rejects ambient light.  
- Red/blue ratiometric measurement compensates for distance and saliva.  
- The optical fiber tip is recessed only 0.3 mm, so it samples a very small, near-contact region.  
- The system can also operate during a pre-brushing “scan” with water only, before toothpaste is applied, if a user wants the cleanest optical map.  
- Use of a low-foam, non-fluorescent toothpaste can further improve real-time sensitivity.

### Challenge 3: Bristles flex continuously

A glass optical fiber would fatigue and break under toothbrush flex cycles.

**Solution:** Use a **polymer optical fiber**, which is flexible and more resistant to repeated bending than silica. The fiber is also potted in a soft silicone strain-relief at the base of the tuft.

### Challenge 4: Electrical safety in the mouth

**Solution:**

- Battery-powered.  
- Galvanically isolated from the charger.  
- Sensing voltage ≤100 mV RMS.  
- Current limited to <10 µA.  
- Conductive bristles are insulated with parylene C except at the small exposed tip.  
- Brush head is sealed to IP67.

### Challenge 5: Making the map useful without a camera

Full 3D tooth mapping from a brush is difficult. The invention uses a **zonal map**, not a pixel-level image.

The handle includes a 6-axis IMU. The app combines brush orientation with the six zone sensors to produce a coarse but clinically useful map: left/right, upper/lower, buccal/lingual, anterior/posterior.

---

## 7. Operating parameters summary

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Sensor zones per brush head | 6 |
| Optical sensor bristle | 1 polymer optical fiber per zone, 250 µm core, NA 0.5 |
| Excitation source | 405 nm LED, 10 kHz modulation |
| Optical power at tip | ≤0.5 mW peak, ≤0.1 mW average during scanning |
| Fluorescence detection | 600 nm long-pass, silicon photodiode |
| Impedance sensing | 50 kHz and 1 MHz, 100 mV RMS, <10 µA |
| Conductive bristle | Carbon-loaded nylon, 0.18 mm diameter, parylene C coated |
| Local actuator | PZT-5A, 5 mm × 0.2 mm, 200–400 Hz |
| Battery | 3.7 V Li-ion, ~500 mAh, wireless charging |
| Wireless | Bluetooth LE 5.0 |
| Brush head replacement | 3 months, like a normal brush head |
| Sealing | IP67 |

---

## 8. Safety and regulatory considerations

### Optical safety

The excitation source is a 405 nm LED, not a laser. Average optical power is below **0.1 mW per sensor fiber**. The beam exits a 250 µm fiber and diverges quickly, so irradiance at the tooth is low. This is not intended to be an ophthalmic device; it operates inside the mouth, and the LED can be off when the head is outside the mouth using a proximity or temperature sensor.

### Electrical safety

The impedance sensor uses AC at low voltage and microamp current, so there is no meaningful tissue stimulation or heating. The brush is battery-powered and isolated from the charger during use.

### Biocompatibility

All oral-contact materials — PMMA fiber, parylene C, carbon-loaded nylon, PEEK, silicone — are selected for ISO 10993 compatibility. The brush head is a consumable and is replaced periodically.

### Regulatory

A commercial product would likely need clearance for plaque detection claims if marketed as a medical device. If marketed only as a wellness tool with “plaque feedback,” the regulatory path is lighter, but clinical validation would still be required.

---

## 9. Concrete utility advantage over existing approaches

Standard electric toothbrushes are **time-based and pressure-based**. They tell the user to brush for two minutes and to avoid pressing too hard. They do not tell the user **where plaque remains**.

The GlimpseBrush core changes brushing from an open-loop behavior into a **closed-loop detection-and-removal process**:

- It detects plaque directly at the tooth surface.  
- It responds immediately with local vibration.  
- It tells the user which zones are clean and which are not.  
- It trains better brushing habits over time.

This is especially valuable for:

- People with orthodontic brackets.  
- People with periodontitis or gingivitis.  
- Elderly or disabled users with poor brushing technique.  
- Children who need objective feedback.  
- Anyone who brushes the prescribed time but still leaves plaque in the same hard-to-reach areas.

Clinical plaque-disclosing tablets already show that many people miss the same areas every day. The difference is that GlimpseBrush provides that feedback **during brushing**, without dyes, without a dental chair, and without a separate camera.

---

## 10. Prototyping path

### Phase 1: Benchtop sensor tuft

Build one sensor tuft on a linear stage. Test on extracted human teeth with controlled plaque/biofilm or a porphyrin-based fluorescent plaque analog.

Measurement goals:

- Red/blue ratio vs. plaque thickness.  
- Impedance shift vs. plaque coverage.  
- Minimum detectable plaque index.

### Phase 2: Multi-zone brush head

Fabricate a brush head with six sensor tufts and wired handle. Evaluate in a dental simulator with artificial plaque.

### Phase 3: Wireless handheld prototype

Miniaturize the optical engine, impedance front end, battery, and Bluetooth into a sealed handle. Test with human volunteers under a dental ethics protocol.

### Phase 4: Clinical study

Compare plaque removal with a standard sonic toothbrush using a Quigley-Hein/Turesky plaque index before and after brushing. The key endpoint is **remaining plaque**, not brushing time.

---

## 11. Why this is faithful to the seed

The seed proposed a smart toothbrush whose bristles detect micro-debris through optical and capacitive sensing and then adjust vibration to target the area. This proposal preserves that exact mechanism, but replaces the physically impossible “sensor in every nylon bristle” with a manufacturable real-world coupler: **dedicated optical-fiber sensor bristles and conductive polymer bristles embedded among ordinary cleaning bristles**.

The result is not a camera-based plaque detector, not a standard pressure-sensing electric brush, and not an app-only tracker. It is a toothbrush that actually senses plaque at the bristle tip and cleans where necessary.

## DebrisGuard Adaptive Sensing Brush Head  
*A real-time, closed-loop bio-sensing toothbrush head with impedance/fluorescence debris classification and adaptive mechanical action*

From the seed, I am isolating the one truly unconventional core: **a brush head that detects and classifies the material on the tooth in real time using micro-capacitive and optical sensors, then changes its brushing motion accordingly.** The water jet, app, UV sanitizer, and eco-material claims are not the central mechanism; they can be optional accessories. The central invention is a **bio-sensing, feedback-driven brush head and actuation system**.

---

## 1. Core concept

The brush head contains six small multimodal sensor nodes distributed across the bristle field. Each node measures two independent physical signatures of the tooth/coating interface:

- **Electrical impedance spectroscopy** via insulated interdigitated microelectrodes, i.e., the “micro-capacitive” sensor concept from the seed.
- **Optical fluorescence and near-infrared reflectance** via small polymer optical fibers.

A small embedded neural network in the handle fuses these signals and classifies the surface state as:

- clean enamel,
- dental plaque/biofilm,
- sugary or starchy food residue,
- sticky fibrous food residue,
- mineralized deposit / calculus-like material,
- soft tissue / gingiva,
- toothpaste foam / saliva only.

The handle then selects the mechanical actuation mode in real time:

| Surface state | Actuation mode |
|---|---|
| Plaque/biofilm | Directional linear strokes, 180–280 Hz, 0.3–0.8 mm amplitude |
| Sugary/sticky residue | Gentle orbital/circular micro-motion, 40–70 Hz, 0.2–0.5 mm radius |
| Sensitive tissue or gingiva | Low-amplitude mode, 60–100 Hz, 0.05–0.15 mm |
| Clean surface | Reduced power / maintenance sweep |

This preserves the seed’s idea of “adjusts pressure, stroke pattern, and duration” without turning it into a generic toothbrush or a simple timer.

---

## 2. Sensor head architecture

### 2.1 Passive sensing brush head

The replaceable brush head is intentionally passive—it contains no batteries, no microcontroller, and no active ICs. This keeps the disposable part inexpensive and more easily recyclable.

Each of the six sensor nodes contains:

- **Interdigitated impedance electrodes**
  - Material: sputtered gold on flexible polyimide/PET substrate
  - Electrode digit width and spacing: 100 µm
  - Active sensing area: approximately 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm
  - Coating: 3–5 µm parylene-C, bio-compatible and electrically insulating
  - Function: forms a fringe-field capacitor that couples to the tooth surface and adjacent fluid/debris film without galvanic contact

- **Optical fiber pair**
  - Two multimode PMMA or cyclic-olefin polymer fibers, 250 µm core
  - One excitation fiber
  - One collection fiber
  - Tips polished at 45° with a protected reflective bevel or embedded in a clear low-fluorescence silicone optical window
  - Tip recessed ~0.2 mm inside a soft silicone pod, avoiding direct tissue contact but still optically coupled to the tooth surface

The sensor pods are made of medical-grade, low-fluorescence silicone, Shore A 50, so they are soft and non-irritating. They are placed between normal nylon bristle tufts. The pods are slightly shorter than the surrounding cleaning bristles—about 7.5 mm versus 8.0 mm—so during normal brushing pressure they contact the tooth surface while the bristles still do the mechanical work.

### 2.2 Head-to-handle connector

The head base includes:

- 12 gold-plated electrical pads for the impedance electrodes
- an optical ferrule containing 12 fiber ends: 6 excitation and 6 collection
- a magnetic mechanical coupling

The handle side uses:

- spring-loaded pogo pins for the impedance channels
- a molded microlens array or expanded-beam optical coupling to align the fibers with handle LEDs and photodiodes

This connector is sealed to IPX7 when the head is attached.

---

## 3. Handle electronics and signal acquisition

The handle contains all active electronics.

### 3.1 Impedance front end

A dedicated impedance analyzer chip, for example the AD5940 or equivalent, multiplexes across the six sensor nodes. It applies a sine wave of approximately **100 mV RMS** at discrete frequencies:

- 1 kHz
- 5 kHz
- 20 kHz
- 100 kHz
- 500 kHz
- 2 MHz
- 5 MHz

At each frequency the system measures complex impedance magnitude and phase. Because the electrodes are coated with parylene-C, the measurement is capacitively coupled. The effective electric field extends into the thin film on the tooth surface, probing:

- ionic conductivity at low frequencies,
- Maxwell-Wagner interfacial polarization in biofilms and food films at mid frequencies,
- dielectric permittivity and water content at high frequencies.

This is not merely “moisture detection.” The shape of the impedance spectrum across the 1 kHz–5 MHz range carries enough information to distinguish:

- saliva and foam,
- sugary residue,
- protein-rich food,
- bacterial biofilm,
- mineralized calculus-like deposit.

### 3.2 Optical front end

Each node has two optical channels:

1. **405 nm fluorescence**
   - Excite with a 405 nm LED or laser diode, mean optical power below 2 mW.
   - Bacterial porphyrins, particularly protoporphyrin IX, fluoresce in the red region, 630–700 nm.
   - The handle photodiode uses a 600 nm long-pass filter.
   - Plaque score = red fluorescence / 405 nm backscatter ratio.

2. **850 nm near-infrared reflectance**
   - Measures scattering and film thickness/density.
   - Helps distinguish air bubbles and foam from actual adherent debris.

The optical excitation is amplitude-modulated at 1 kHz, and the photodiode signal is demodulated with synchronous lock-in detection. This rejects ambient light and slow-changing background signals.

### 3.3 Processing and AI

The handle uses a low-power microcontroller with a small neural-network accelerator, for example an STM32N6-class part or equivalent Arm Cortex-M33 + NPU.

Input features:

- 6-frequency impedance magnitude and phase per node
- 405 nm fluorescence ratio
- 850 nm reflectance ratio
- contact flag derived from capacitive change
- 3-axis accelerometer / gyroscope data
- motor current and position estimate
- applied-force estimate

The classification model is a small 1D convolutional neural network or gradient-boosted tree ensemble, quantized to int8, with fewer than ~50,000 parameters. It runs at 5–10 Hz, producing a class label and a risk score for each node.

The response latency from sensor reading to actuator change is under 200 ms.

---

## 4. Adaptive mechanical actuation

The brush head is not driven by a conventional single-mode motor. Instead, the handle contains a compact two-axis flexure stage.

### 4.1 Two-axis flexure actuator

- Moving mass: head + shaft ≈ 12–15 g
- Suspension: glass-filled PEEK or stainless steel cross-flexure
- Two miniature voice-coil actuators arranged at 90° to one another
- Each axis is driven by a controlled current source with back-EMF position estimation
- The flexure is tuned to have a resonance near 200–260 Hz for efficient linear oscillation

This two-axis stage can produce:

- **Linear directional strokes:** drive one axis at 180–280 Hz, amplitude 0.3–0.8 mm
- **Orbital/circular micro-motion:** drive both axes at 40–70 Hz with 90° phase separation, radius 0.2–0.5 mm
- **Sensitive mode:** low amplitude 0.05–0.15 mm at 60–100 Hz

A passive tuned mass damper inside the handle suppresses reaction forces, reducing hand vibration even during high-frequency linear mode.

### 4.2 Pressure sensing and limiting

A strain-gauge or piezoelectric force sensor in the neck measures axial brushing force. If the user exceeds approximately 2.0–2.5 N, the handle:

- reduces actuation amplitude,
- activates a haptic alert,
- optionally changes LED color.

This directly addresses enamel abrasion and gingival recession caused by over-brushing.

---

## 5. Key engineering challenge and solution

The hardest problem is making a stable measurement in a wet, vibrating, foam-filled, noisy environment while a user presses the head against teeth.

Solutions:

1. **Capacitive coupling instead of direct electrical contact.**  
   The parylene-coated electrodes prevent electrochemical reactions, electrode fouling, and any shock risk.

2. **Differential impedance measurements.**  
   Adjacent nodes are compared to suppress common-mode changes caused by saliva temperature, salinity, and foam.

3. **Contact-flag gating.**  
   The system estimates whether each node is actually touching or optically coupled to a tooth. Frames with no contact are excluded from classification.

4. **Lock-in optical detection.**  
   The 1 kHz optical modulation rejects ambient light, slow thermal drift, and many toothpaste foam fluctuations.

5. **Soft sensor pods.**  
   The sensing elements are mounted in flexible silicone, allowing them to conform to curved tooth surfaces without scratching enamel or causing injury.

6. **Passive disposable head.**  
   All active electronics stay in the handle, improving reliability and reducing head cost and e-waste.

---

## 6. Materials and operating parameters

### Brush head

- Body: PLA/PHA blend or bio-derived aliphatic polyamide, formulated to remain hydrolytically stable for at least 12 months of normal use and then degrade in industrial compost
- Bristles: nylon 6/12 or bio-based nylon, 0.12–0.15 mm diameter
- Sensor pod: low-fluorescence medical-grade silicone, Shore A 50
- Electrodes: gold on polyimide/PET, parylene-C coating
- Optical fibers: PMMA or cyclic-olefin polymer, 250 µm core

### Handle

- Enclosure: recycled ocean plastic / post-consumer polycarbonate blend, sealed to IPX7
- Battery: rechargeable Li-ion, 3.7 V, 1000 mAh, Qi wireless charging
- Connectivity: Bluetooth Low Energy 5.0
- MCU: Arm Cortex-M33 with NPU
- Impedance analyzer: AD5940 or equivalent
- Actuator: two-axis voice-coil flexure stage
- Inertial sensing: 9-axis IMU for position/orientation tracking

### Optical safety

- 405 nm excitation: mean power below 2 mW
- 850 nm source: below 1 mW
- No UV light is emitted into the mouth
- Optional UV-C sanitizing only occurs in a closed charging case with interlocks

### Electrical safety

- Impedance drive voltage: 100 mV RMS
- Electrode leakage current: below 10 µA
- All tissue-contacting electrodes are fully insulated with parylene-C

---

## 7. Utility advantage over existing approaches

Conventional powered toothbrushes are essentially **blind and uniform**. They vibrate or oscillate at one setting, regardless of whether they are cleaning plaque, grinding sugar residue into fissures, or overbrushing exposed dentin.

Existing plaque detection tools, such as disclosing tablets or dental fluorescence cameras, show plaque but do not clean it. They are also not integrated into the brushing loop.

DebrisGuard closes the loop:

1. It detects plaque and food debris while brushing.
2. It adapts the mechanical action to the actual material.
3. It avoids aggressive high-frequency brushing on sensitive or soft tissue.
4. It provides objective, location-specific feedback after the session, rather than merely timing a 2-minute cycle.

For users with orthodontic brackets, implant-supported crowns, gingivitis, exposed dentin, or high caries risk, this mechanism is genuinely useful because it targets biofilm where it actually exists and reduces mechanical damage where it is not needed.

---

## 8. Prototype development path

A prototyping sequence would be:

1. **Benchtop sensor validation**  
   Build a single-node impedance/optical probe and test it against artificial tooth surfaces coated with:
   - Streptococcus mutans biofilm
   - sucrose solution
   - egg-yolk/starch food residue
   - hydroxyapatite calculus analog
   - artificial saliva

2. **Sensor array integration**  
   Fabricate a six-node passive head and connector, and integrate it with the handle electronics.

3. **Actuator characterization**  
   Build the two-axis flexure actuator and measure stroke amplitude, frequency response, and hand vibration with a laser displacement sensor and accelerometer.

4. **Classification training**  
   Collect labeled impedance and optical data under realistic in vitro brushing conditions, including toothpaste foam, saliva, and varying temperature.

5. **Cleaning efficacy study**  
   Compare plaque removal and food-debris removal against a standard sonic toothbrush in a typodont model with identical brush time and head geometry.

6. **Clinical pilot**  
   A small human feasibility study measuring plaque index reduction, gingival irritation, and user acceptance.

---

From the original broad product idea, this is the part worth building: a passive, multi-sensor brush head that truly detects debris type and a two-axis actuator that changes its cleaning motion in response. It preserves the seed’s core mechanism while making it physically feasible and prototype-ready.

## GlowBite Micro-Debris Evacuation Brush Head  
### Selected seed concept: “Micro-Debris Removal Technology” — nano-coated flexible filaments + integrated mini-vacuum that pulls debris from between teeth and below the gumline

I’m developing only the most unusual, physically nonstandard part of the original GlowBite idea: the **suction-assisted micro-debris removal system**. Existing smart brushes already use pressure sensors, apps, AI timers, and colored LEDs. The genuinely novel mechanism is putting a safe, low-pressure micro-aspiration system directly into the brush head so that loosened plaque and food particles are **transported out of the mouth**, especially from interproximal spaces and the gingival sulcus.

The literal idea of “ultra-suction below the gumline” is not safe or practical: high vacuum could trap gingival tissue, cause hematomas, or fail because the port seals against mucosa. Therefore, I preserve the seed’s suction paradigm by engineering a **non-sealing, pressure-limited micro-aspiration coupler** that creates gentle outward fluid flow at the gumline.

---

## 1. Core physical principle

The device combines two physical processes:

1. **Mechanical loosening** — flexible, nano-textured bristle filaments disrupt plaque biofilm and debris on enamel and at the gingival margin.
2. **Micro-aspiration transport** — a regulated negative pressure at ports located at the base of the bristle tufts pulls air, saliva, and loosened particles into a collection chamber.

The suction is not meant to “vacuum” the tissue. It is intended to create a gentle pressure gradient from the interproximal space and gingival sulcus toward the port, carrying debris outward.

---

## 2. System architecture

### 2.1 Brush head

The head is an engineered single-use/replaceable module containing:

- **Bristle field**  
  - Conventional nylon tufts for surface brushing.  
  - Added flexible, tapered filaments at the tip and sides for interproximal access.  
  - Filament core: nylon 612, base diameter 0.15 mm, tip tapered to 0.05–0.08 mm.  
  - Surface nano-texture formed by plasma etching or food-grade polymer nanotexturing, then coated with a 50–150 nm silicone/plasma-fluoropolymer coating for low friction, low biofilm adhesion, and reduced plaque re-deposition. No free nanoparticles are used.

- **Suction manifold**  
  - Molded into the head body.  
  - 6–10 aspiration ports, each 0.5–0.8 mm diameter, located near the gingival margin and at the base of bristle tufts.  
  - Ports feed into one central low-flow channel that connects to the handle.

- **Sulcus-access coupler**  
  - A soft silicone element at the brush-head edge, made from 30 Shore A medical-grade silicone.  
  - It has a 0.5 mm depth stop so it cannot be inserted deeply below the gumline.  
  - The aspiration orifice is 0.6 mm, surrounded by multiple 0.3 mm side vents.  
  - The side vents prevent the port from sealing against gingiva or cheek tissue. If tissue touches the port, air leaks through the vents and suction collapses locally.

### 2.2 Handle

The handle contains:

- **Miniature peristaltic pump**  
  - Pump type: miniature rotary peristaltic or piezoelectric diaphragm pump.  
  - Handles mixed air/saliva/debris without the pump contacting the debris.  
  - Flow rate: 10–25 mL/min.  
  - Port pressure target: **−5 to −8 kPa** (−38 to −60 mmHg).  
  - Pressure relief valve opens at approximately −9 kPa to prevent excessive vacuum.

- **Debris collection chamber**  
  - Transparent, removable 5 mL cup.  
  - Contains a 100 µm nylon mesh filter to trap debris and protect the pump.

**Invention proposal:** **“Glimpse” — an opto-acoustic, bristle-waveguide toothbrush that detects debris per tooth section**

I’m isolating the seed’s most unusual and paradigm-shifting idea: **the toothbrush itself senses debris at the bristle tips using optical and micro-acoustic waves.** I am not developing the app, gamification, or eco-bristles as the core invention here; those are supporting features. The core is the physical sensing architecture.

The literal seed idea—tiny electronic sensors embedded in each bristle tip—is not physically manufacturable: bristles flex millions of times, sit in saliva/oil/dentifrice, and cannot support semiconductor junctions, wires, or power delivery at their tips. But the seed’s underlying physical principle can be preserved exactly by turning the bristle tips into **passive optical and acoustic waveguides**. The tip remains the sensing point; the actual transducers sit remotely in the brush head or handle.

---

## 1. Core physical mechanism

The brush uses two co-located sensing modalities per tooth section:

1. **Optical spectroscopy through a bristle-like optical fiber**  
   - 405 nm light excites bacterial porphyrins in plaque/biofilm, producing red fluorescence around 600–700 nm.  
   - Healthy enamel and clean tooth surfaces produce green autofluorescence around 500–550 nm.  
   - 850 nm and 633 nm reflectance provide information about food particles, surface scattering, and debris thickness.

2. **Micro-acoustic pulse-echo through a bristle-like titanium acoustic waveguide**  
   - A 20 MHz ultrasonic pulse travels down a thin titanium wire.  
   - At the tip, the pulse crosses a thin saliva/film gap and reflects from the soft debris layer or hard enamel.  
   - A clean enamel surface gives a strong, fast echo.  
   - A soft plaque/biofilm layer creates an additional weak first reflection and attenuates the enamel echo.  
   - A sticky sugar/carbohydrate film strongly damps the echo and shifts the echo spectrum downward.  
   - Hard calculus/tartar gives a high-amplitude, rigid-surface echo.

By fusing the optical and acoustic signatures, the brush distinguishes:

- clean enamel
- bacterial plaque/biofilm
- sticky sugar-rich/carbohydrate film
- food debris
- calculus/tartar
- uncertain/ambiguous surface

This is not a standard “smart toothbrush” that merely tracks brush motion with an accelerometer. It directly interrogates the material on the tooth surface.

---

## 2. Physical architecture

### 2.1 Brush head and sensing nodes

The brush head contains **six opto-acoustic sensing nodes** distributed along the head. Each node corresponds to a tooth-section-sized area under the brush.

Each node consists of:

- **One optical sensing fiber**  
  - Material: low-fluorescence fused silica or low-fluorescence PMMA  
  - Core diameter: 200 μm  
  - Outer diameter with cladding: 230 μm  
  - Outer nylon jacket: 350 μm  
  - Numerical aperture: 0.22  
  - Tip: rounded, cleaved, and overcoated with a thin low-index medical-grade silicone layer  
  - The tip is recessed about **0.3 mm** behind the outer cleaning bristle tips.

- **One acoustic waveguide wire**  
  - Material: medical-grade Ti-6Al-4V ELI titanium alloy  
  - Diameter: 200 μm  
  - Coating: 5 μm parylene C  
  - Tip: rounded and coated with a 20–30 μm medical epoxy or parylene matching layer  
  - The tip is also recessed about **0.3 mm** behind the outer bristle tips, so it does not scrub enamel.

- **One passive piezoelectric transducer**  
  - Material: PZT-5A or PZT-5H  
  - Dimensions: approximately 1.0 mm × 1.0 mm × 0.1 mm  
  - Operated in thickness mode at a center frequency of **20 MHz**  
  - Bonded to the proximal end of the titanium acoustic waveguide with a thin, hard epoxy bond line <5 μm  
  - Air-backed on the rear face to maximize acoustic output.

- **A surrounding tuft of ordinary nylon cleaning bristles**  
  - Material: nylon 6-12  
  - Diameter: 0.15 mm  
  - End-rounded and polished  
  - These perform the actual mechanical scrubbing, while the optical/acoustic waveguides remain recessed.

Each node is made as a small module: a 1.5–2.0 mm diameter polycarbonate or medical-PEEK ferrule holds the optical fiber and titanium waveguide. The cleaning bristles are injection-molded or staked around that ferrule. The module can then be inserted into the brush head.

The six nodes are arranged so that as the brush sweeps over teeth, each node sees a small region roughly covering one to two teeth. Because the head is replaceable, the nodes can be tuned for different arch sizes.

### 2.2 Neck connection

The brush head has no active semiconductor electronics. This keeps the replaceable head inexpensive and reduces e-waste.

The neck connector contains:

- **A multimode optical ferrule**  
  - A 6-fiber MT-style ferrule aligns all six optical fibers at once.  
  - Spring-loaded physical contact maintains optical coupling with the handle.  
  - An O-ring seal keeps moisture out of the optical interface.

- **Pogo-pad electrical contacts for the six PZT transducers**  
  - Seven gold-plated pads: six signal lines plus one common ground.  
  - The PZT transducers are passive, so the head only needs electrical traces on a thin Kapton flex circuit.

- **A mechanical latch**  
  - Standard replaceable-head locking feature.

Because the head contains only fibers, titanium wires, passive PZT elements, nylon bristles, and plastic, it can be replaced every three months without discarding complex electronics.

### 2.3 Handle electronics

The handle contains:

- **Optical engine**
  - Light sources:
    - 405 nm LED, not a laser, to reduce speckle and eye/oral safety concerns  
    - 633 nm LED  
    - 850 nm LED  
  - A 1×6 multimode MEMS fiber switch routes the shared optical engine to each sensing node sequentially.  
  - A dichroic beamsplitter separates emission light from returned fluorescence/reflectance.  
  - Three filtered photodiodes:
    - Green channel: 500–550 nm  
    - Red fluorescence channel: 620–700 nm  
    - NIR reflectance channel: 800–880 nm  
  - LEDs are modulated at 10 kHz and lock-in detection is used to reject ambient room light and 50/60 Hz lighting.

- **Acoustic front end**
  - High-voltage pulser: 5–15 V pulses, 100 ns width, 1 kHz repetition rate  
  - Transmit/receive switch  
  - Low-noise amplifier  
  - Bandpass filter centered at 20 MHz  
  - 100 MS/s ADC for echo capture

- **Processor**
  - Arm Cortex-M4F-class MCU with DSP instructions  
  - Runs the TinyML debris classifier locally  
  - No cloud connection required for real-time classification

- **Motion sensing**
  - 6-axis MEMS accelerometer/gyroscope  
  - Used to map sensor readings to intraoral positions

- **Battery and charging**
  - Sealed rechargeable Li-ion cell, e.g., 3.7 V, 2000–2500 mAh  
  - USB-C charging with overvoltage, overcurrent, and thermal protection  
  - No replaceable batteries

- **Motor**
  - Standard oscillating-sonic or sonic toothbrush actuator  
  - Motor operation is synchronized with the sensing sequence to reduce vibrational noise during acoustic measurements.

---

## 3. How the optical sensing works

During a sensing burst, the 405 nm LED illuminates the tooth surface through the 200 μm optical fiber. The fiber tip is recessed 0.3 mm behind the cleaning bristles, so it does not touch enamel. A thin saliva layer of roughly 0.1–0.5 mm remains between the fiber tip and the tooth.

At 405 nm:

- Bacterial plaque emits red fluorescence because of porphyrins such as protoporphyrin IX.
- Healthy enamel emits green autofluorescence.
- The ratio of red fluorescence to green autofluorescence is a well-established indicator of plaque/biofilm presence. This is the same principle used in quantitative light-induced fluorescence, but here it is shrunk into a bristle-coupled waveguide.

At 633 nm and 850 nm:

- Colored food particles such as tomato, spinach, or berry residues reflect differently from clean enamel.
- 850 nm is relatively insensitive to pigment and provides a scattering/roughness reference.
- A thick, opaque food film scatters or attenuates the returned signal.

The same optical fiber collects the backscattered and fluorescent light. The handle optical engine separates the spectral bands and measures their intensities.

To prevent toothpaste foam from corrupting the optical measurement, the primary optical scan is done **before toothpaste application** on wet teeth, or after rinsing. During foam-filled brushing, the system relies on the saved debris map and periodic brief checks when the acoustic path is interpretable.

---

## 4. How the micro-acoustic sensing works

The PZT transducer launches a 20 MHz, two-cycle ultrasonic pulse into the titanium waveguide. Titanium has high acoustic impedance, so the pulse travels efficiently along the wire. The wire is surrounded by a low-durometer silicone cladding to prevent acoustic leakage into the brush head.

At the tip, the pulse radiates into the saliva/film layer. It then encounters a series of interfaces:

- saliva → soft plaque/film  
- soft plaque/film → enamel

Because the acoustic impedance of enamel is high—about 16 MRayl—and saliva is about 1.5 MRayl, a clean enamel surface produces a strong reflection with a short round-trip time.

When a soft plaque biofilm is present:

- The saliva-to-biofilm interface gives a weak first echo because the impedance difference is small.
- The biofilm-to-enamel echo is delayed and attenuated.
- The echo train shows a small initial peak followed by a reduced enamel peak.

When a sticky sugar-rich film is present:

- The sugar film is not necessarily a distinct impedance mismatch, but its high viscosity and acoustic attenuation damp the high-frequency pulse.
- The enamel echo amplitude drops.
- The echo becomes broader.
- The spectral centroid shifts to lower frequencies.

The device is calibrated using sucrose solutions in artificial saliva at 37°C, covering low-viscosity saliva up to high-viscosity sugar films. A thermistor near the head corrects for temperature because saliva viscosity and acoustic attenuation depend on temperature.

Acoustic features extracted from each pulse-echo trace include:

- amplitude of the first film echo
- amplitude of the enamel echo
- round-trip time-of-flight
- spectral centroid
- spectral bandwidth
- echo decay constant

These features are compared against stored reference signatures for clean enamel, plaque, sugar film, food debris, and calculus.

The acoustic mode is non-cavitational and non-destructive. It does not remove plaque or calculus; it only measures. The ultrasonic pressure at the tip is below 0.1 MPa, so there is no cavitation, no erosion, and no heating risk.

---

## 5. Data fusion and classification

Each node produces a feature vector roughly like this:

**Optical features**
- Red fluorescence intensity under 405 nm
- Green autofluorescence intensity under 405 nm
- Red/green ratio
- 633 nm reflectance
- 850 nm reflectance
- Optical scattering index

**Acoustic features**
- First echo amplitude
- Enamel echo amplitude
- Enamel echo time-of-flight
- Spectral centroid
- Spectral bandwidth
- Echo decay constant

A small machine-learning classifier—e.g., a quantized random forest or a small feedforward neural network—runs directly on the handle MCU. Inference takes a few milliseconds.

Output classes:

1. Clean enamel  
2. Bacterial plaque/biofilm  
3. Sticky carbohydrate/sugar film  
4. Food debris  
5. Calculus/tartar  
6. Uncertain

The classification is per node. During a 5–10 second mapping sweep before brushing, the handle records node data at 20 Hz while the IMU tracks brush position and orientation. The result is a **debris heat map** of the user’s mouth, showing which zones have plaque, sticky sugar film, food debris, or calculus.

The brush can then adjust its cleaning mode: if the user moves over a flagged zone, the handle may extend the brushing time, alter the motor speed, or give haptic feedback until the sensor indicates that the zone has been cleaned.

---

## 6. Key engineering challenges and how they are solved

### Challenge 1: Literal sensors in each bristle tip are impossible

**Solution:** The bristle tips are not electronic sensors. They are passive optical fibers and metallic acoustic waveguides. The actual light sources, photodetectors, piezoelectric drivers, and amplifiers are in the handle or at the proximal end of the head. The distal tip remains the sensing point, preserving the seed’s “bristle-tip sensor” concept in a manufacturable form.

### Challenge 2: Toothpaste foam blocks optical and acoustic signals

**Solution:** The system uses three phases:

1. **Pre-brush scan:** No toothpaste. The user wets the brush and performs a 5–10 second sweep. The brush builds the debris map.
2. **Guided cleaning:** Toothpaste is applied. The brush uses the saved map and IMU to guide the user. It may periodically pause for acoustic spot checks if conditions allow.
3. **Post-rinse scan:** After rinsing, the user can do a final scan to confirm that flagged zones are now clean.

### Challenge 3: Brush vibration corrupts the micro-acoustic echo

**Solution:** The acoustic measurement is either performed during 100–200 ms motor pauses, or the measurement is phase-locked to the motor drive signal. For a prototype, short motor pauses are simpler and robust.

### Challenge 4: Sensor bristles would wear if they touched enamel

**Solution:** The optical fiber tip and titanium waveguide tip are recessed 0.3 mm behind the surrounding nylon bristles. Under normal brushing force, the sensor tips remain separated from enamel by a thin saliva gap. Ordinary nylon bristles do the mechanical work.

### Challenge 5: Detecting sugar residue specifically

**Solution:** Sugar is optically transparent and non-fluorescent in the visible range, so a direct optical “sugar sensor” would be unreliable. The acoustic mode detects a sticky, high-viscosity carbohydrate film by its strong damping and spectral downshift of the ultrasound echo. The system therefore reports **sticky sugar-like residue** rather than an exact milligram-per-milliliter sucrose measurement. This is still clinically meaningful because it identifies the kind of retentive film that promotes caries.

---

## 7. Operating parameters

### Optical subsystem

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Excitation wavelengths | 405 nm, 633 nm, 850 nm |
| Fiber core diameter | 200 μm |
| Fiber NA | 0.22 |
| Tip standoff from enamel | 0.1–0.5 mm |
| Optical power at tip | ≤0.2 mW |
| Spot diameter on tooth | ~0.3–0.5 mm |
| Optical irradiance | <500 mW/cm² |
| Detection bands | 500–550 nm, 620–700 nm, 800–880 nm |
| Modulation | 10 kHz lock-in |

The 405 nm source is a visible violet LED, not ultraviolet. This avoids the photochemical and genotoxic concerns associated with UV sources.

### Acoustic subsystem

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Center frequency | 20 MHz |
| Pulse width | 100 ns, ~2 cycles |
| Pulse repetition frequency | 1 kHz |
| Drive voltage | 5–15 V |
| Acoustic pressure at tip | <0.1 MPa |
| Mechanical index | <0.03 |
| ADC sampling rate | 100 MS/s |
| Averaging | 32 pulses per measurement |

The acoustic output is diagnostic-level, not therapeutic. It does not produce cavitation, thermal damage, or enamel erosion.

---

## 8. Materials and safety

### Biocompatibility

All mouth-contacting materials must meet ISO 10993-1 and food-contact standards:

- Optical fiber jacket: medical-grade nylon or polyurethane  
- Optical tip coating: medical-grade low-index silicone  
- Acoustic waveguide: Ti-6Al-4V ELI with parylene C coating  
- PZT transducer: encapsulated, with no exposed lead  
- Brush head housing: medical polycarbonate or polysulfone  
- Neck seal: medical silicone O-ring  
- Cleaning bristles: nylon 6-12, end-rounded

### Electrical safety

- The intraoral portion is passive or low-voltage.  
- The handle battery is sealed.  
- USB-C charging includes overvoltage, overcurrent, short-circuit, and thermal protection.  
- No mains power is used during brushing.

### Therapeutic safety

- No ultrasound cavitation.  
- No UV.  
- No sensor tip touching enamel.  
- No sharp edges at the fiber or titanium tips.

---

## 9. Utility advantage over existing approaches

Traditional toothbrushes are blind. The user cannot know whether a particular molar groove was actually cleaned.

Most “smart” toothbrushes add motion tracking, pressure sensors, and timers. They infer cleaning from brush movement. They do not measure whether plaque, sugar film, or food debris actually remains on the tooth surface.

Plaque-disclosing tablets stain plaque but are messy, do not distinguish sticky sugar film, and cannot be used continuously during brushing.

Camera-based dental scanners and intraoral cameras can image plaque, but they require a separate wand, good line-of-sight, and often a dentist or hygienist.

The Glimpse architecture offers:

- **Direct material-specific feedback** from the tooth surface.
- **Detection of transparent sticky sugar films**, which optical-only plaque detectors would miss.
- **No messy disclosing dyes.**
- **No external camera wand.**
- **In-brush operation**, so it fits within a normal brushing routine.
- **A replaceable head with no expensive electronics**, because all active optical and acoustic processing remains in the reusable handle.

This is especially useful for:

- children who need precise brushing guidance  
- elderly people with reduced manual dexterity  
- caregivers brushing someone else’s teeth  
- orthodontic patients whose brackets and wires trap debris  
- people with high caries risk who need to identify sugar-retentive zones

---

## 10. Prototyping roadmap

### Stage 1: Benchtop single-node validation

Build a single opto-acoustic probe using:

- a 200 μm silica optical fiber  
- a 200 μm titanium wire  
- a PZT-5A transducer  
- a 405 nm LED  
- a spectrometer or filtered photodiodes

Test on:

- hydroxyapatite disks  
- extracted human teeth  
- artificial saliva  
- sucrose films at 10–60 wt%  
- cultured Streptococcus mutans biofilm  
- food particles such as tomato paste, spinach, and chocolate

Measure:

- red/green fluorescence ratio  
- acoustic echo amplitude and spectral shift  
- classification accuracy versus known sample identity

### Stage 2: Six-node brush head

Build a prototype brush head with six sensing nodes arranged for tooth-section coverage. Connect the nodes to benchtop electronics using a temporary cable bundle.

Validate:

- node-to-node repeatability  
- crosstalk between adjacent nodes  
- signal quality during brushing-like motion  
- acoustic performance with motor vibration

### Stage 3: Miniaturized handle

Package the optical engine, acoustic front end, MCU, IMU, motor driver, and battery into a waterproof handle. Use an MT optical ferrule and pogo-pad connector for the detachable head.

### Stage 4: Clinical feasibility study

Conduct a small study with 20–30 volunteers. Compare the Glimpse debris map with:

- dental examination by a hygienist  
- plaque-disclosing tablet photography  
- quantitative light-induced fluorescence

Evaluate usability, safety, and classification agreement.

### Stage 5: Regulatory

A first-generation product can be positioned as a **wellness aid** with “debris detection” and “cleaning guidance.” If the manufacturer wants to claim detection of plaque or caries risk, additional clinical validation and regulatory review—such as FDA 510(k) in the United States or CE marking under MDR in Europe—would be required.

---

## 11. What makes this invention genuinely different

The seed’s real insight was not “put a computer in a toothbrush.” The real insight was the idea of sensing debris **from inside the bristle tips themselves**, using optical and micro-acoustic signatures.

This proposal preserves that exact physical paradigm through a real-world coupler: the bristle tips become passive optical and acoustic waveguides. The optical fiber bristle delivers light and collects fluorescence. The titanium bristle delivers an ultrasonic pulse and collects the echo. The system combines those signals to distinguish plaque, sticky sugar films, food debris, and calculus per tooth section.

That direct material-specific, in-brush sensing is the property that no standard motion-tracking smart toothbrush currently provides.
